module_title: Preamble & Salient Features - Judicial Interpretations and Complex Dynamics
introduction: This advanced level explores the deep jurisprudential significance of the Preamble, the Supreme Court's changing stance on its constitutional status, the Basic Structure Doctrine, and the unique synthesis of parliamentary sovereignty with judicial supremacy.

core_concepts.title: Is Preamble a part of the Constitution?
core_concepts.description: In the Berubari Union Case (1960), the Supreme Court ruled that the Preamble is NOT a part of the Constitution. However, in the landmark Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973), the SC reversed its stance and held that the Preamble IS a part of the Constitution and can be amended.

core_concepts.title: The Basic Structure Doctrine
core_concepts.description: Emerged from the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973). It states that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution (including Fundamental Rights and the Preamble) under Article 368, provided it does not alter or destroy the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

core_concepts.title: Synthesis of Parliamentary Sovereignty & Judicial Supremacy
core_concepts.description: India blends the British principle of parliamentary sovereignty with the American principle of judicial supremacy. The Supreme Court can declare parliamentary laws unconstitutional (Judicial Review), while Parliament can amend the major portion of the Constitution.

core_concepts.title: Integrated and Independent Judiciary
core_concepts.description: Unlike the USA, India has a single integrated judicial system (Supreme Court at the top, High Courts below) that enforces both Central and State laws. Independence is secured through fixed service conditions and security of tenure.

core_concepts.title: Emergency Provisions
core_concepts.description: A highly unique feature where the federal structure automatically converts into a unitary one during national emergencies, without requiring a formal constitutional amendment.

important_entities.name: Kesavananda Bharati
important_entities.significance: His case against the Kerala government led to the Supreme Court establishing the 'Basic Structure Doctrine', saving Indian democracy from absolute parliamentary dictatorship.

important_entities.name: Granville Austin
important_entities.significance: Described the Indian federalism as 'Cooperative Federalism'. He noted that the Constitution is a 'seamless web' uniting the nation.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Although the Preamble is a part of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has clarified that it is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a prohibition upon the powers of the legislature.

Western secularism implies a complete separation between religion and the state (Negative concept). Indian secularism embodies a 'Positive concept'—giving equal respect and protection to all religions (Sarva Dharma Sambhava).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Chronology of cases: Berubari (1960) = NOT a part. Kesavananda (1973) = IS a part. LIC of India (1995) = INTEGRAL part.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Assertion-Reasoning questions, perfectly align the 'Basic Structure Doctrine' with the limitation on Parliament's amending power under Article 368.
Be prepared to identify which features of the Constitution fall under the 'Basic Structure' (e.g., Secularism, Rule of Law, Judicial Review).
